The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.misconception: Takes a reform plea for praise of the system it attacks.
options.text: He praises the encomienda system as fundamentally fair and just.

options.misconception: Confuses Las Casas with the colonists he condemns.
options.text: He argues that Native peoples possessed no rights whatsoever under Spain.
He stresses Spanish greed and cruelty to make reform seem urgent.

options.misconception: Assumes an advocate spares the people he blames.
options.text: He avoids blaming any Spaniards so the Crown will not take offense.

rationales.A: The passage condemns the colonists, it does not praise them. Las Casas calls their conduct greed and cruelty, not fairness.
rationales.B: Las Casas spent his career arguing that Native peoples did possess natural rights. The passage defends their humanity, it does not deny it.
rationales.C: Las Casas wrote as an advocate for reform. He stresses greed and cruelty because shocking the Crown was his way to make reform seem urgent.
rationales.D: The passage blames the Spaniards directly, naming their ambition and avarice. It does not spare them to protect the Crown's feelings.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who Las Casas is writing to. The passage is addressed to the Crown, asking it to act.
2. Ask what he wants. He wants the Crown to reform colonial policy and curb the cruelty.
3. Read the passage as a tool for that goal. Every line stresses greed, cruelty, and suffering.
4. Rule out the rest. He does not praise the system, deny Native rights, or spare the colonists.
Remember: when a writer asks a ruler to act, read the passage as persuasion, not as a neutral report.

stem: Las Casas wrote the passage above to persuade the Spanish Crown to reform its colonial policies. How does that purpose shape the passage?

stimulus.source_note: Bartolome de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321. Archaic spelling kept.
stimulus.text: Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more facil and easie) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth.
